entry.title: Deterministic Guardrails: Prompts Steer, Hooks Enforce
entry.summary: A loop that refactors code until a check passes is a few lines of shell. Most guardrails beside such a loop only watch what an agent already wrote; the one worth building refuses a bad edit before it lands, and that is what this piece constructs. The rule it enforces: production code under src/ must not import a mock library. That rule can live in two places. Put it in the prompt, do not import mock, and it is clear and still only a request: text loaded into a model is a lever on probability, not a switch, so it leaves the model free to write the import anyway. Put it in a gate that fires before a write lands, and it refuses the edit outright. Both state the same rule; only one can make it hold every time. The ask channel has a ceiling: a prompt pushes the odds up, never to one. How close …

entry.summary: AFP — Advanced Function Presentation — predates the web. It came out of IBM in the 1980s, moves to production printers over IPDS, and still composes a huge share of the world's bank statements, insurance documents, and healthcare EOBs. entry.title: A structurally valid USPS barcode can still encode garbage — validating IMb from the bars
entry.summary: Every piece of US commercial mail carries an Intelligent Mail barcode — 65 vertical bars, each in Here's the part that surprised me when I built a validator: most "IMb checks" only verify that Sixty-five bars, four valid states each, plausible geometry — pass. The USPS spec (USPS-B-3200) defines the pipeline roughly like this: The tracking + routing fields pack into a single large integer via positional arithmetic (the routing code contributes up to ~10^11 of the space — this is effectively base conversion with mixed radixes). An 11-bit frame check sequence (CRC) is computed over that integer's byte representation. The integer is converted into ten 3-digit codewords (more base conversion).
